mainTopic: Guarding the ears from improper speech, and the question of a first marital union with a בתולה on שבת
overview: The amud opens by finishing a teaching about the ear: a person who hears something improper should plug his ears with his finger. The גמרא ties this to רבי אלעזר's question of why fingers look like pegs. It first rejects reading the question as being about fingers being separate, since each finger already has its own job. The real point is that fingers are pointed like pegs, so they can plug the ears. A ברייתא from דבי רבי ישמעאל adds that the soft earlobe can be folded in for the same purpose. Another ברייתא warns not to listen to idle talk. Then the גמרא opens a new topic: may a man have a first union with his בתולה bride on שבת? It builds a chain of questions: is the blood stored or part of the body, does he want the blood, the opening, or his own pleasure, is the opinion of רבי שמעון or רבי יהודה followed for an unintended act, and is the act destructive or constructive. A second version of this chain (איכא דאמרי) is still going when the amud ends, and it continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Put your finger in your ears
steps.stepSummary: The end of a teaching: someone who hears improper words should put his finger in his ears.
steps.simpleTranslation: He should place his finger in his ears.
steps.whatsHappening: This line finishes a teaching that started just before this section. Someone who hears something improper should plug his ears with his finger.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The teaching started earlier with בר קפרא's reading of the פסוק 'ויתד תהיה לך על אזנך'. He read it as 'a peg on your ear', so your finger acts like a peg to block your ear. This line gives the practical result.

keyTerms.meaning: finger
ears
a peg (the word behind this teaching)

phrases.english: he should place his finger in his ears.
phrases.notes: This finishes a sentence from before this section: if a person hears something improper, he should plug his ears.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes a teaching that started before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When a person hears something improper, he should block his ears with his finger.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר asks why fingers look like pegs
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא links the teaching to רבי אלעזר's question about why fingers resemble pegs.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is what רבי אלעזר said: Why are a person's fingers similar to pegs?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says this matches a question asked by רבי אלעזר. He asked why our fingers are shaped like pegs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'והיינו' means 'this is the same idea as'. The finger-as-peg teaching fits with רבי אלעזר's question. His answer is not given yet; the גמרא will first figure out what exactly he was asking.

keyTerms.meaning: and this is the same as / this matches
pegs

phrases.english: And that is what Rabbi Elazar said:
Why are the fingers of a person
similar to pegs?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the finger-in-ear teaching with a matching statement from רבי אלעזר.
steps.raayaObject: The idea that fingers are meant to work like pegs for blocking the ears.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי אלעזר's question about why fingers look like pegs.

steps.title: What did רבי אלעזר mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what exactly רבי אלעזר's question was about.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what רבי אלעזר meant when he compared fingers to pegs. This sets up the next steps, which test two possible meanings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Fingers are like pegs in more than one way. They are separate from each other, and they are pointed. The גמרא wants to know which likeness רבי אלעזר had in mind.

keyTerms.meaning: what is the reason?

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks what רבי אלעזר meant in step 2.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: In what way are fingers like pegs, according to רבי אלעזר?

steps.title: Not about fingers being separate
steps.stepSummary: Reading the question as 'why are fingers separate?' is rejected, because each finger plainly has its own job.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say the question is why they are separate from each other, that is obvious: each one is made for its own purpose. As the Master said: this one is for a זרת, this one for a קמיצה, this one for an אמה, this one is the אצבע, and this is the thumb.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries one reading: maybe רבי אלעזר asked why fingers are separate, like a row of pegs. It rejects that reading, because we already know why: each finger has its own special job.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the question were about separateness, there would be nothing to ask. A known teaching lists a holy job for each finger, such as measuring a זרת, taking a קמיצה from a מנחה, and measuring an אמה. So רבי אלעזר must have been asking something else.

keyTerms.meaning: if you would say (a suggestion about to be rejected)
that they are separate from each other
a span (pinky to thumb), used as a measure
a fistful taken from a מנחה
thumb

phrases.english: If we say it is because they are separate from each other,
each and every one was made for its own matter.
As the Master said: This is for a span,
this is for a fistful, this is for a cubit,
this is the finger, this is the thumb.
phrases.notes: Here 'אצבע' means one particular finger, the pointer, not fingers in general.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests a first answer to the question in step 3 and rejects it.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only this reading of רבי אלעזר's question, not the question itself.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The reason fingers are separate is already known, since each has its own job, so there would be nothing to ask.
steps.confusionAlert: The list of fingers is not the answer to רבי אלעזר. It shows why the 'separate fingers' reading can't be right. The real answer comes in the next step.

steps.title: Pointed like pegs to plug the ears
steps.stepSummary: The real question is why fingers are pointed like pegs: so a person can plug his ears against improper speech.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the question is why they are pointed like pegs. The answer: so that if a person hears something improper, he can put his fingers in his ears.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the correct reading of רבי אלעזר's question. Fingers are pointed so they can fit into the ears and block out improper words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the comparison is about shape, not separateness. A pointed peg fits into a hole, and a finger fits into the ear. This brings us back to the teaching in step 1.

keyTerms.meaning: rather (switching to the correct reading)
pointed, tapered
an improper, unfitting thing

phrases.english: Rather: what is the reason they are pointed like pegs?

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאִם יִשְׁמַע אָדָם דָּבָר שֶׁאֵינוֹ הָגוּן,
phrases.english: So that if a person hears an improper matter,
he will place his fingers in his ears.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected reading from step 4 with the correct one.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי אלעזר was asking why fingers are pointed like pegs, and the answer is so they can block the ears from improper speech.
steps.whatToRemember: Fingers are 'like pegs' because they are pointed, so a person can block his ears from improper words.

steps.title: The soft earlobe can seal the ear
steps.stepSummary: דבי רבי ישמעאל teach that the ear is hard but the lobe is soft, so the lobe can be folded in to block improper speech.
steps.simpleTranslation: A sage from the school of רבי ישמעאל taught: Why is the whole ear hard and the earlobe soft? So that if a person hears something improper, he can fold the earlobe into the ear.
steps.whatsHappening: A ברייתא from דבי רבי ישמעאל gives a similar teaching. The soft earlobe is made to be folded into the ear to block out improper speech.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This teaching is like the finger teaching but uses a different body part. It shows the same idea again: the body was built so we can protect ourselves from hearing bad things.

keyTerms.meaning: a sage from the study hall of רבי ישמעאל taught
earlobe (here)
he should bend / fold

phrases.english: A sage of the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught:
Why is the entire ear hard
and the earlobe soft?
phrases.notes: Usually אַלְיָה means the fat tail of a sheep. Here it means the soft lobe of the ear.

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאִם יִשְׁמַע אָדָם דָּבָר שֶׁאֵינוֹ הָגוּן,
phrases.english: So that if a person hears an improper matter,
he will bend the earlobe into it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a matching teaching about the earlobe.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The soft earlobe is there so a person can fold it in and block improper speech.

steps.title: Do not listen to idle talk
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא warns not to let one's ears hear idle talk, because the ears are the first limbs to be burned.
steps.simpleTranslation: The rabbis taught: A person should not let his ears hear idle words, because they are the first of the limbs to be burned.
steps.whatsHappening: A ברייתא gives a general warning: don't listen to empty, useless talk. The reason is that the ears are the first part of the body to be burned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This goes further than the earlier teachings. Those were about improper speech; this one also covers plain idle talk. The ears are very sensitive, so a person must guard what goes into them.

keyTerms.meaning: idle, useless talk
are burned

phrases.english: The Sages taught:

phrases.aramaic: אַל יַשְׁמִיעַ אָדָם לְאׇזְנָיו דְּבָרִים בְּטֵלִים,
phrases.english: A person should not let his ears hear idle matters,
because they are the first of the limbs to be burned.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: אַל יַשְׁמִיעַ אָדָם לְאׇזְנָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the ear section with a general warning.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person should not listen to idle talk, since the ears are the first limbs to be burned.
steps.whatToRemember: The body is built to help us block bad speech: pointed fingers and a soft earlobe. We should guard our ears even from idle talk.

steps.title: Is a first union allowed on שבת?
steps.stepSummary: A new question: may a man have a first union with his בתולה bride on שבת? It depends on whether the blood is just stored or is part of the body.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: What is the law about having a first union on שבת? Is the blood simply stored there, or is it attached to the body?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic with an איבעיא. It asks whether a first union is allowed on שבת, and frames it as a question about the blood that comes out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the blood is just stored, letting it out is not a wound, so there may be no problem. If it is attached to the body, letting it out makes a חבורה, a wound, which is forbidden on שבת.

keyTerms.meaning: a question was asked before them (an open question)
to have a first marital union (with a בתולה)
is simply stored / pooled
is attached (so releasing it makes a wound)

phrases.english: A question was raised before them:
What is the law about a first union on Shabbat?
Is the blood just stored there,
or is it attached?
phrases.notes: If it's attached to the body, drawing it out counts as making a wound, which is a problem on שבת.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ: מַהוּ לִבְעוֹל בַּתְּחִלָּה בְּשַׁבָּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, back to the laws of marrying a בתולה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is the blood of a first union stored blood, which is fine to release, or attached blood, which makes a forbidden wound on שבת?
steps.whyThisMatters: This question about blood and wounds shapes the whole discussion that follows about marrying a בתולה near שבת.

steps.title: If the blood is stored: does he want the blood or the opening?
steps.stepSummary: Even if the blood is stored, another question remains: is he after the blood (allowed) or the opening (forbidden)?
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say the blood is stored: does he need the blood, so it is allowed? Or maybe he needs the opening, so it is forbidden?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a second question in case the blood turns out to be stored. Now it asks what the husband's real goal is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If what he wants is the blood coming out, that is just releasing stored blood, so it is allowed. But if what he wants is the opening, then making the opening is a forbidden act on שבת. So the ruling depends on his purpose.

keyTerms.meaning: and if you conclude (a follow-up question)
an opening
permitted
forbidden

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם תִּימְצֵי לוֹמַר דָּם מִיפְקָד פְּקִיד:
phrases.english: And if you say the blood is just stored:
does he need the blood, and so it is permitted?

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִּלְמָא לַפֶּתַח הוּא צָרִיךְ, וַאֲסִיר.
phrases.english: Or perhaps he needs the opening, and so it is forbidden?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִם תִּימְצֵי לוֹמַר דָּם מִיפְקָד פְּקִיד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds a second layer on the question in step 8, for the case where the blood is stored.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is the husband's goal the blood, which is allowed, or the opening, which is forbidden on שבת?
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think this question is pointless once we say the blood is stored. Even with no wound, making the opening could still be forbidden on שבת. That is why the גמרא asks it.

steps.title: If he wants only the blood, is the opening an unintended act that is allowed?
steps.stepSummary: Suppose he only needs the blood and the opening happens by itself. Do we follow רבי שמעון, who permits an unintended act, or רבי יהודה, who forbids it?
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say he needs the blood, and the opening just comes about by itself: is the הלכה like רבי שמעון, who says an unintended act is permitted, or like רבי יהודה, who says an unintended act is forbidden?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא takes the 'allowed' side of the last question (he only wants the blood) and asks a new question on top of it. The opening still happens, even though he does not intend it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Making the opening is the forbidden part, but here it is only a side effect of what he wants. That is the classic case of דבר שאין מתכוין. So now the answer depends on the famous argument between רבי שמעון and רבי יהודה.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you say (we accept one side of the previous question; now a new question follows)
It comes by itself, as a side effect
An unintended act: a permitted action that may cause a forbidden result he did not want
The opening

steps.confusionAlert: Notice the switch: in step 9, wanting the blood was the 'allowed' side. Here the גמרא shows it may still be a problem, because the opening happens anyway.
steps.whyThisMatters: The argument between רבי שמעון and רבי יהודה about דבר שאין מתכוין comes up all over שבת, so this ties the case into a major general rule.

phrases.english: And if you say
he needs the blood
and the opening comes about by itself
is the halacha like Rabbi Shimon
who said an unintended act is permitted
or is the halacha like Rabbi Yehuda
who said an unintended act is forbidden?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִם תִּימְצֵי לוֹמַר לַדָּם הוּא צָרִיךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the 'he wants the blood' side of step 9 and asks the next question built on it.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether an unintended forbidden result (the opening) is permitted, as רבי שמעון holds, or forbidden, as רבי יהודה holds.

steps.title: Even following רבי יהודה, is making the opening destructive or constructive?
steps.stepSummary: Even if the halacha follows רבי יהודה, maybe the opening is a destructive act, which is not a forbidden מלאכה, or maybe it is a constructive act.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say the halacha is like רבי יהודה: is he destroying with regard to the opening, or fixing with regard to the opening?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds one more layer. Even if unintended acts are forbidden, we still have to know what kind of act making the opening is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On שבת, a purely destructive act (מקלקל) is not a real forbidden מלאכה. Only a constructive act (מתקן) is. If making the opening counts as damage, it would be allowed even according to רבי יהודה.

keyTerms.meaning: One who damages or destroys; such acts are not a forbidden מלאכה on שבת
One who fixes or improves something, a constructive act
With regard to

phrases.english: And if you say
the halacha is like Rabbi Yehuda
is he destroying with regard to the opening
phrases.notes: A destructive act is not counted as a forbidden מלאכה on שבת, so that would make it allowed.

phrases.english: or is he fixing with regard to the opening?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִם תִּימְצֵי לוֹמַר הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the strict side of step 10 (רבי יהודה) and asks whether the act is still allowed because it is destructive.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether making the opening is a destructive act (allowed) or a constructive act (forbidden).
steps.whatToRemember: First version of the chain: Is the blood stored? → Does he want the blood or the opening? → רבי שמעון or רבי יהודה? → Destructive or constructive?

steps.title: Second version: if the blood is part of the body, does he want the blood or only his pleasure?
steps.stepSummary: Some say the chain goes differently. If the blood is part of the body, drawing it is a wound. Does he want the blood, which would be forbidden, or only his own pleasure, which would be permitted?
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: And if you say the blood is attached to the body, does he need the blood, so it is forbidden? Or perhaps he needs it only for his own pleasure, so it is permitted?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second version of the chain of questions. This version takes the other side of step 8: the blood is part of the body.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the blood is part of the body, bringing it out is like making a wound, which is forbidden on שבת. So the question becomes his intention. If he wants the blood, that is forbidden. If he only wants his own pleasure, it is permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: It is attached, part of the body
His own pleasure
It is permitted

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a continuation of steps 10-11. It is a different version of the same chain, starting from the other side of step 8.

phrases.english: Some say
And if you say
the blood is attached to the body
does he need the blood, and so it is forbidden

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִּלְמָא לַהֲנָאַת עַצְמוֹ הוּא צָרִיךְ
phrases.english: or perhaps he needs it for his own pleasure
and so it is permitted?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי: וְאִם תִּימְצֵי לוֹמַר דָּם חַבּוֹרֵי מִיחַבַּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Restarts the chain from step 8 with an alternate version, taking the 'blood is part of the body' side.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: If the blood is part of the body, whether his aim is the blood (forbidden wounding) or only his pleasure (permitted).

steps.title: If he wants only his pleasure, does the halacha follow רבי יהודה or רבי שמעון?
steps.stepSummary: If he only wants his pleasure and the blood comes out by itself, we are back to the argument about unintended acts: רבי יהודה or רבי שמעון?
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say he needs it for his own pleasure, and the blood comes out by itself: is the halacha like רבי יהודה or like רבי שמעון?
steps.whatsHappening: In the second version, the גמרא takes the 'permitted' side (only pleasure) and asks the next question. The blood still comes out even though he does not intend it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the forbidden result is the bleeding, which is a wound, and it happens without his intent. That makes it a דבר שאין מתכוין. So again the answer depends on whether we follow רבי יהודה (forbidden) or רבי שמעון (permitted).

keyTerms.meaning: And the blood comes out by itself, as a side effect

steps.whatToRemember: Second version of the chain: The blood is part of the body → Does he want the blood or only pleasure? → If only pleasure, רבי יהודה or רבי שמעון? Both versions end up depending on the rule of דבר שאין מתכוין.

phrases.english: And if you say
he needs it for his own pleasure
and the blood comes out by itself
is the halacha like Rabbi Yehuda
or is the halacha like Rabbi Shimon?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִם תִּימְצֵי לוֹמַר לַהֲנָאַת עַצְמוֹ הוּא צָרִיךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the 'only his pleasure' side of step 12 and applies the רבי יהודה / רבי שמעון question, as step 10 did in the first version.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the unintended bleeding is forbidden, as רבי יהודה holds, or permitted, as רבי שמעון holds.

steps.title: Is causing the wound destructive or constructive?
steps.stepSummary: Suppose the הלכה follows רבי יהודה, so an unintended act is forbidden. We still need to know whether causing this wound counts as a מקלקל בחבורה (a destructive wound) or a מתקן בחבורה (a constructive wound).
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say the הלכה follows רבי יהודה, is he being destructive in making the wound, or constructive in making the wound?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא climbs one more step on the ladder of questions. It accepts the stricter view of רבי יהודה for now. Then it asks what kind of act the wounding is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if an unintended act is forbidden, there must be a real forbidden מלאכה behind it. A wound that only damages may not count as a real מלאכה, while a wound that builds something does. So the question shifts from intent to the nature of the act itself.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you say (if the earlier question is decided this way)
One who destroys; a damaging act
One who fixes or improves; a constructive act
A wound that draws blood

steps.confusionAlert: Step 11 asked a similar 'destructive or constructive' question about the opening. Here, in the second version of the chain, the same question is asked about the wound (חבורה).

phrases.english: And if you say
the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda,
phrases.notes: So an unintended act is forbidden. That's the stricter side of the question in step 13.

phrases.english: is he destructive in making the wound
or is he constructive in making the wound?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִם תִּימְצֵי לוֹמַר הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the strict side of step 13 (רבי יהודה) and asks the next question in the chain.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the wound made here counts as a destructive wound or a constructive wound.

steps.title: For destructive acts, which view does the הלכה follow?
steps.stepSummary: Suppose the wound is destructive. The גמרא now asks whether, for destructive acts, the הלכה follows רבי יהודה, who exempts a destructive act. The other side of the question continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say he is destructive in making the wound, then for destructive acts, does the הלכה follow רבי יהודה...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds another rung to the ladder. It assumes the wound is destructive and starts asking whose view we follow for destructive acts. The question is only half finished here, so this step sets up the next move.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the wound is destructive, the question becomes whether a destructive wound is still punishable. רבי יהודה's view, mentioned here, exempts a destructive act. The other side of the question comes on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: In the case of a destructive act
The binding ruling follows (someone's view)

phrases.english: And if you say
he is destructive in making the wound,
in destructive acts, does the halacha follow Rabbi Yehuda,

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִם תִּימְצֵי לוֹמַר מְקַלְקֵל בְּחַבּוּרָה הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the 'destructive' side of step 14 and asks the next question in the chain.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether, for destructive acts, the הלכה follows רבי יהודה, who exempts them, or the opposing view that comes next.
